title: Consistent Hashing
summary: Add or remove nodes without moving almost every key.
keyPoints: Modulo hashing remaps most keys when the node count changes.
A hash ring assigns each key to the next node clockwise.
Adding or removing a node moves only the keys in its arc.
Virtual nodes smooth the distribution and spread load during failures.
Consistent hashing balances keys, not request rate; hot keys still need caches or splitting.

complexity.note: v is the number of virtual nodes.
Only the new node's arc is copied.
Keys go to the next node clockwise.
A node-count change remaps most keys.

commonMistakes: Using one ring position per node and assuming the load will be even.
Expecting consistent hashing to fix a hot key; it only distributes keys.
Changing ring membership quickly without a plan for replica repair and client refresh.
Hashing a request id instead of an entity key, which destroys locality.
interviewNotes: Explain the modulo failure with a one-line example before drawing the ring.
Mention virtual nodes and why they matter.
State the replication rule: owner plus the next distinct nodes clockwise.
Say when a directory or modulo hash is the simpler choice.

checkYourself.question: Why does modulo hashing move so many keys when a node is added?
checkYourself.answer: The modulus changes, so almost every key gets a different remainder. Even a small change in node count can remap the majority of the key space.

checkYourself.question: What do virtual nodes solve?
checkYourself.answer: They give each physical node many positions on the ring, which smooths the share of keys it owns and spreads its load across many neighbors when it leaves.

checkYourself.question: Does consistent hashing remove hotspots?
checkYourself.answer: No. It balances keys across nodes, but a single key with very high request volume still lands on one owner and needs caching, splitting, or dedicated capacity.
